item.title: Shaping the Menu: Information Design under Screening
item.description: arXiv:2610.14225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How should consumers learn when a seller chooses a menu of product qualities and prices? We study information design when the seller observes the learning policy, but not consumers' private signals, before choosing its menu. Under cost-curvature conditions, we characterize optimal learning when consumer surplus receives greater weight than profit. Even with two valuations, every optimal posterior distribution combines an interval of posterior types with an efficiently served atom at the highest valuation. The induced menu features a continuum of differentiated products. Strikingly, optimal learning can also induce a lower posterior atom, separated from this interval by a support gap. Buyers in this atom either purchase an isolated low-quality product or are excluded, even when trade with every buyer creates gains. Both configurations can be optimal for the same prior and welfare weight. Served buyers with distinct posterior types are never bunched at the same quality. General finite priors can yield several separating regions and trading atoms. We also characterize the optimal joint design of learning and valuation-dependent segmentation, showing, among other results, that every posterior type with positive gains from trade must be served. Joint design can raise both consumer surplus and profit relative to buyer-optimal private learning alone. Even random assignment to segments with different learning policies and separate menus can give consumers more surplus than any single market yielding the same profit. Additional price discrimination can therefore benefit consumers, even when privacy restrictions require segmentation to reveal nothing about valuations to the seller.
item.dc:creator: Panagiotis Kyriazis

item.title: Optimal Dynamic Majority-Quorum Rules: Theory and Evidence
item.description: arXiv:2610.14391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the optimal sequential aggregation of randomly arriving votes from a finite population to identify an unknown majority preference before a fixed deadline, trading off decision accuracy against the cost of delay. The optimal policy is a dynamic majority-quorum rule: a joint, time-varying threshold on vote lead and count, in which quorum and supermajority requirements emerge as the solution to an inference problem about non-participants' preferences. At each date, the continuation region is lens-shaped: the lead required to stop grows with turnout until too few voters remain to overturn it, and it vanishes at the deadline. We characterize conditions under which the boundary is monotone in the stakes, the arrival process, and time. Because the exact boundary admits no closed form, we derive a large-population approximation that reduces the two-dimensional rule onto a single sufficient statistic, and express the rule as a sequential significance test set by a single error tolerance. Calibrated on Polkadot governance data, an out-of-sample evaluation finds that our rule with a 2\% error tolerance halves decision times relative to the incumbent mechanism.
item.dc:creator: Bhargav Nagaraja Bhatt, Jonas Gehrlein, Kremena Valkanova

item.title: Robust Capital Budgeting
item.description: arXiv:2610.14569v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study capital budgeting when a manager privately knows project productivity and her empire-building benefits, while headquarters lacks credible priors. Headquarters minimizes maximum regret relative to informed investment. Without compensation, the optimal policy is a spending cap balancing empire-building overinvestment against profitable investment forgone. Compensation helps when empire-building incentives are weak. The optimal payment incentivizes restraint, declines with investment, and reaches zero at the spending cap, supporting greater managerial discretion. When empire-building incentives are strong, compensation cannot distinguish productive investment from biased expansion; therefore, a spending cap alone is optimal.
item.dc:creator: Yunzhi Hu, Fei Li, Hanqing Ye, Dihan Zou

item.title: Allocative Efficiency and the Returns to Innovation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14969v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When producers in a network compete in quantities, an innovator's profit contains none of the change in allocative efficiency that its innovation causes, whether a gain or a loss, because its own choices are optimal and other effects on its profit are transfers. A process innovator also forgoes its own and downstream markups on the output its innovation adds at a fixed allocation, worth 14 to 26 percent of its cost saving for U.S. public firms in 2015. For innovators accounting for 68 percent of sales, the change in allocative efficiency exceeds a tenth of the private return. In a Markov R&D game, reallocation of R&D across firms is likewise external to the innovator. Rivals' profits and market values can misstate the welfare cost of business stealing from them even in sign. With estimated spillovers, the social return to R&D is 5.39 times the private return, against 2.53 in output-based accounting with estimated business stealing, mainly because that accounting credits the innovator with its rivals' lost sales.
item.dc:creator: Koki Okumura

item.title: Coalition-Proof Disclosure
item.description: arXiv:2610.15087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study generalized verifiable disclosure by an informed sender with type-independent preferences. We first characterize all perfect Bayesian equilibria as individually rational partitions of the sender's types into coalitions ordered by payoff. An equilibrium survives our coalition-proofness criterion if no group of types can profitably coordinate an announcement that the receiver will interpret as coming precisely from the types willing to join it. Coalition-proof equilibria are partitions that are greedy: at each step, a coalition of the remaining types attains the highest payoff consistent with equilibrium. Given the generality of our setting, coalition-proof equilibria may fail to exist. We establish existence under restrictions on preferences and evidence: quasiconcavity with message completeness, betweenness, cheap talk with message completeness, and payoff degradation. For a rich disclosure game with stochastic evidence, we show that the sender's ex-ante payoff in a coalition-proof equilibrium is a piecewise linear tent over the belief simplex, analogous to the concave closure in Bayesian persuasion and the quasiconcave closure in cheap talk.
item.dc:creator: Germ\'an Gieczewski, Maria Titova

item.title: Resource Allocation with Midterm Review
item.description: arXiv:2610.15786v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A principal funds an agent's project over two periods, with a midterm review providing a public signal about project quality. The agent privately knows the project's quality and always prefers more funding, while the principal wants to match funding to quality. A natural benchmark uses the review only after it arrives, to update beliefs and improve the second-period allocation. The optimal mechanism instead frontloads the review's information value: it also uses the review as an incentive device to elicit truthful reporting up front, thereby strictly improving the principal's first-period expected payoff. In the optimal mechanism, higher-quality projects receive more funding initially but face larger cuts after a bad review, leaving them with less funding than lower-quality projects. A good review increases funding, but the resulting allocation need not preserve the initial ranking of projects and eventually declines with quality.
item.dc:creator: Yijun Liu

item.title: Continuity of stable marriage correspondences
item.description: arXiv:2610.17460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a continuum version of the stable marriage problem, in which each agent has a variable mass to be paired to the opposite side. An agent's mass is interpretable as the divisible time of a single atomistic agent, or as a mass of infinitesimal agents of a particular type. Our object of interest is the mapping between the vector of masses to the set of stable matches. As in the canonical stable marriage model, the set of stable matches can be multi-valued, so this mapping is a correspondence. This correspondence is continuous if and only if the stable match is unique, implying that small changes in the masses may cause discontinuous jumps in the set of stable matches.
item.dc:creator: Will Sandholtz, Andrew Tai

item.title: AI Information Synthesis and Content Polarization
item.description: arXiv:2610.17674v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can synthesize dispersed information into balanced and informative content, raising the possibility that AI may help reduce polarization. We show that this promise can be undermined by the strategic response of content producers. We develop a game-theoretic model in which consumers acquire information to make downstream decisions, content producers allocate limited informational capacity between broadly valuable vertical information and horizontally differentiated information, and AI provides an alternative source of synthesized information. The effects of AI unfold in three phases as its reliability increases. When reliability is low, AI has no effect on the market. At intermediate levels, AI disciplines prices without attracting consumers or changing content. When AI becomes sufficiently reliable, consumers begin to substitute toward it, and content producers respond by shifting informational capacity away from the vertical dimension and toward horizontally differentiated content, thereby increasing content polarization. The mechanism operates through audience composition: AI attracts consumers who are less well matched to individual producers, leaving producers with stronger incentives to cater to their remaining audiences. The polarization effect intensifies with AI reliability but weakens with greater competition among content producers. Our findings highlight a potential wedge between AI's direct and equilibrium effects: a technology that provides consumers with more balanced information can indirectly make the broader content ecosystem more polarized.
item.dc:creator: Chang Liu, Yuting Zhu

item.title: More Goods Means More Commitment
item.description: arXiv:2610.18581v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A seller without commitment to future offers interacts with a buyer over time. There are many goods for sale, with the buyer's value for a bundle the sum of each bundled good's value. Each date, the seller jointly announces a menu of subsets of the remaining inventory and current prices, and the buyer may purchase one of the offered subsets or wait. In the next period, the seller may again offer any menu of the remaining goods. Neither buyer nor seller can commit to future behavior. I show that as players become maximally patient, if scope increases sufficiently fast compared to patience, revenue per good converges to expected value per good and buyer utility per good converges to zero, in any equilibrium. But if patience instead grows sufficiently fast compared to scope, seller revenue per good converges to the lowest possible value and the buyer captures all remaining surplus, in any equilibrium.
item.dc:creator: Mark Whitmeyer

item.title: Falsification-proof non-market allocation mechanisms
item.description: arXiv:2610.18625v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Relying on manipulable characteristics to target the allocation of resources is fraught with difficulties. Naively optimal rules lead to falsification and allocative inefficiency. Optimizing the rule for allocative efficiency while accounting for falsification typically induces falsification, at a heavy cost to the agents. Moreover, falsification generates negative externalities. We characterize optimal falsification-proof rules under a broad range of falsification technologies. We also provide an honesty condition under which they solve the unconstrained problem of a planner who maximizes a weighted sum of allocative surplus and agents' welfare.
item.dc:creator: Eduardo Perez-Richet, Vasiliki Skreta

item.title: Multilateral governance of invasive alien species management: An ecological-economic model with Allee effect
item.description: arXiv:2610.14916v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Invasive alien species (IAS) generate substantial ecological and economic damages that often transcend political boundaries, creating strong incentives for coordinated management. We develop a two-region ecological-economic model of IAS control that integrates prevention and eradication measures with population dynamics characterized by logistic growth and an Allee effect. We derive analytical results on the interaction between ecological thresholds and strategic behaviour and compare outcomes under cooperation (central planner) and non-cooperation (open loop Nash equilibrium and Markovian Nash equilibrium). We show that, under realistic control costs, neither prevention nor eradication can eliminate invasive populations in finite time, and complete prevention of cross-border spread is generally not optimal. In the absence of an Allee effect, the zero-population equilibrium is unstable, implying long-run persistence of the invasive species. By contrast, the presence of an Allee effect fundamentally alters system dynamics by making extinction locally stable and creating a basin of attraction within which eradication becomes feasible. This finding highlights the economic significance of ecological thresholds and demonstrates how delays in management can shift populations beyond critical levels, after which eradication is unlikely regardless of subsequent control efforts. Numerical simulations further show that cooperative management expands the set of initial conditions leading to eradication and consistently reduces aggregate social costs relative to decentralized management. The results provide a formal rationale for rapid intervention, precautionary regulation, and stronger multilateral cooperation in IAS management, particularly in jurisdictions such as the European Union where listing and control actions may be delayed pending evidence of harm.
item.dc:creator: Raouf Boucekkine, Weihua Ruan, Ullrika Sahlin

item.title: Better together? A performance theory of human-machine skill policies under generalization difficulty
item.description: arXiv:2610.16863v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Organizations pairing a human and a machine on a task decide, often by default, which executes each instance and what happens when both do. We account for what this attains under the squared rule, with performance distributed over instances to capture generalization difficulty. A gross stake lies between the skills' mean and best per instance. It splits at the best single skill into a systematic part, known from separate assessments and secured by commitment, and a residual, the expected value of perfect information on which skill each instance favors, known only from paired observation and split further by classes. Skills set the stake; workflows decide the take, via two channels. Routing directs work, weighting or selecting responses; with binary truth it is capped by the best skill per instance. Reading responses as joint evidence is not routing; what they jointly reveal caps it. Synergy lets skills interact before responding; bounded by no skill either way, its lift over independent responses must clear a break-even and can fall below one. As algorithms, arrangements form a ladder stating what each reads, holds and records, and a procedure whose checks keep earlier gains when class means are known and lose little on finite records given a margin. The theory extends to many skills, each worth what it adds where it beats all others held, and to competing skills, where at parity a single failure's allowed cost decides. In a public chest-radiograph study with 227 radiologists, they are near parity with the model and the stake is mostly residual; assisted reading, no better on average originally, returned less than averaging both responses; recalibrating the model alone beats any deployable arrangement of raw responses. Organizations can learn from their records what is at stake, which arrangement collects it and what evidence each step needs; pricing costs and errors is future work.
item.dc:creator: Riccardo Zanardelli

item.title: Unit-Demand Pricing for Min-Buying Customers
item.description: arXiv:2610.17450v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the unit-demand pricing problem under \textit{min-buying} behavior, where customers purchase the lowest-priced item that yields non-negative utility. In contrast to the quasi-linear model, we show that uniform pricing becomes substantially more effective under min-buying. First, we study symmetric environments. We show that for min-buying customers with independent and identically distributed valuations, a uniform price across items is optimal. We then extend this optimality result to all valuations drawn from exchangeable and affiliated distributions. However, uniform pricing is not optimal in all symmetric environments: for min-buying customers we construct an exchangeable and non-affiliated valuation distribution for which the gap between uniform pricing and optimal item pricing is logarithmic in the number of items. This gap is tight and matches the worst-case gap in the quasi-linear setting. Next, we consider asymmetric environments in which valuations are independent but not identically distributed. When these valuations are regular and customers are min-buying, we show that a uniform price guarantees approximately 69.86\% of the optimal item-pricing revenue and this is tight. Overall, our results highlight that the value of non-uniform pricing substantially diminishes, and often disappears entirely, under more conservative demand models in which customers engage in satisficing behaviors such as min-buying.
item.dc:creator: Titing Cui, Michael Hamilton, Jourdain Lamperski, Kasra Tari

item.title: The Geography of (Concurrent) Block Proposing
item.description: arXiv:2610.18812v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The resilience and censorship resistance of a blockchain depend on where the validators and proposers of that blockchain physically operate. We study the economic incentives behind this location choice, both with a single proposer and with multiple concurrent proposers. Formally, we study a game where proposers first choose locations and then compete in a first-price auction for an opportunity whose common value is driven by information from geographically dispersed sources. A single proposer minimizes variance-weighted delay, locating at a weighted median of the sources and co-locating with any dominant one. By contrast, with two proposers, information both observe equally early earns no rent, and each proposer's expected profit is proportional to the standard deviation of the information it receives before its rival. We show that the location game admits the jointly unobserved variance as an ordinal potential, so global solutions of a weighted two-median problem are equilibria. With two sources, one proposer locates at each, however weak one is. With more proposers and at least as many sources, equilibrium locations are distinct under regular bidding. Multiple concurrent proposers thus do more than limit any single proposer's control over inclusion: by rewarding exclusive rather than shared information, they create an economic force toward geographic decentralization.
item.dc:creator: Ciamac C. Moallemi, Mallesh M. Pai, Dan Robinson, Christoph Schlegel

item.title: The Limits of Tolerance
item.description: arXiv:2501.00578v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: I propose a model of aggregation of intervals relevant to the study of legal standards of tolerance. Using this model, I introduce the family of endpoint rules, which aggregate intervals according to the p-th lowest lower endpoint and the q-th highest upper endpoint. This family includes extreme tolerance (allowing anything permitted by anyone) and a form of majoritarianism (the median rule). I show that the family of endpoint rules is characterized by both the combination of anonymity, responsiveness, continuity, and ordinal neutrality, and the combination of anonymity, strategyproofness, and translation equivariance.
item.dc:creator: Alan D. Miller

item.title: Local Strategy-proofness and Dictatorship
item.description: arXiv:2507.00913v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate preference domains on which every unanimous and locally strategy-proof social choice function (scf) is dictatorial. We identify a condition on domains, connected with distinct neighbours, that is necessary for this property. We then show that the condition is also sufficient on L-tops-only domains, i.e., domains on which every unanimous and locally strategy-proof scf is tops-only. Whether every connected with distinct neighbours domain is L-tops-only remains open; if some are not, our sufficiency result is silent on them. We show, however, that every connected with distinct neighbours domain, L-tops-only or not, is a dictatorial domain, i.e., unanimity and strategy-proofness (a stronger requirement than local strategy-proofness) force dictatorship on it.
item.dc:creator: Abinash Panda, Anup Pramanik, Ragini Saxena

item.title: Endogenous Vindication: Reputation and Effort in Expert Advice
item.description: arXiv:2508.19676v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Does making advice cheaper to implement increase the supply of advice? We study an expert who can release a favorable certificate to a sequence of clients. Implementation requires the certificate, and its outcome depends on client effort. The expert values client surplus and career income from routine employment; ability is unknown to both the expert and the public. A lower fixed implementation cost weakly increases both advice and client surplus. A lower marginal effort cost can have the opposite effect: greater effort makes failure more revealing and can induce the expert to withhold advice permanently. We establish this reversal for every discount factor on an open family with smooth income utility with constant absolute risk aversion. At a common initial reputation, cheaper effort then eliminates public learning and client surplus. The reversal is impossible when the effort rule is held fixed across the same cost change. Rare outside reports preserve the discounted client-surplus reversal, although recurrent informative reports restore eventual learning. Additional shape restrictions yield a reputation cutoff; without them, advice can be disconnected and even success can stop further evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Georgy Lukyanov, Anna Vlasova

item.title: Persuasion under the Threat of Verification
item.description: arXiv:2508.19682v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies persuasion when public information is costly and receivers can verify the state before acting. Verification may overturn acceptance after favorable public news, but it may also induce acceptance after unfavorable news. We characterize how these two effects shape the sender's optimal experiment. Cheaper verification can lead the sender to disclose less and rely more on receivers' own discoveries, thereby increasing its payoff. With heterogeneous decision thresholds, we identify exact conditions for the disclosure response and show why it depends on the distribution of preferences. In a separate parameter region, cheaper verification increases inspection but reduces every threshold type's final information and welfare; the sender also loses. We then allow receivers to share their findings. Cheaper inspection and wider sharing can move optimal public disclosure in opposite directions, even when both benefit the sender. Wider sharing can also reduce aggregate final information while improving every threshold type's welfare. The results distinguish the effects of verification on public disclosure, information ultimately obtained, and the cost of obtaining it.
item.dc:creator: Georgy Lukyanov, Samuel Safaryan

item.title: Identity-Compatible Auctions
item.description: arXiv:2511.00723v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies sellers' and buyers' incentives to engage in shill bidding in single-object auctions. An auction is seller identity-compatible if the seller cannot profit by posing as one or more bidders through fictitious identities, and buyer identity-compatible if no buyer can profit by posing as multiple bidders. We distinguish lit auctions, which reveal the number of bidders, from dark auctions, which conceal it. Our results highlight the importance of concealing the number of bidders in deterring shill bidding: no optimal lit auction can achieve our design goal, whereas the dark first-price auction uniquely does.
item.dc:creator: Haoyuan Zeng

item.title: Screening with Advertisements
item.description: arXiv:2601.22404v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate a seller's revenue-maximizing mechanism in a setting where a desirable good is sold together with an undesirable bad (e.g., advertisements) that generates third-party revenue. The buyer's private information is two-dimensional: valuation for the good and willingness to pay to avoid the bad. Building on the duality framework of Daskalakis, Deckelbaum, and Tzamos (2017), whose results extend to our setting, we formulate the seller's problem using a transformed measure $\mu$ that depends on the third-party payment $k$. We provide a near-characterization for optimality of three pricing mechanisms commonly used in practice -- the Good-Only, Ad-Tiered, and Single-Bundle Posted Price -- and introduce a new class of tractable, interpretable two-dimensional orthant conditions on $\mu$ for sufficiency. Economically, $k$ yields a clean comparative static: low $k$ excludes the bad, intermediate $k$ separates ad-tolerant and ad-averse buyers, and high $k$ bundles ads for all types.
item.dc:creator: Kolagani Paramahamsa

item.title: Designing Markets for Screening: Optimal Composition and the Geometry of Surplus
item.description: arXiv:2604.09340v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We characterize the structure of market compositions that generate Pareto efficient outcomes and the geometry of the surplus set in a screening model with type-dependent costs. Maximizing principal or total surplus concentrates the market at the highest type, with all surplus extracted. Agent-oriented optima instead use, rather than suppress, screening: all agents in the market are served, there is no bunching, and a positive share of agents have the highest type and are served efficiently. Separation is valuable even under agent surplus maximization because it propagates information rents. Under a mild cost-curvature condition, each Pareto efficient outcome is implemented by a unique market. Under a stronger cost-curvature condition, the surplus set is convex whenever values are private, or types with no gains from trade can be included in the market. We characterize all surplus outcomes in these cases. Without such types and with type-dependent costs, the surplus set can be nonconvex. Market segmentation generates the missing outcomes but does not increase the maximum agent surplus at any level of principal surplus. We also derive comparative statics along the Pareto frontier and with respect to value-cost co-movement, distinguishing changes in market composition from changes in individual allocations and rents.
item.dc:creator: Panagiotis Kyriazis

item.title: Pricing Intelligence: Task-Based Learning and Labor Displacement in the AI Economy
item.description: arXiv:2608.11112v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: What determines the speed of AI-driven labor displacement? I study this question in a microeconomic model in which users choose between labor and AI to complete tasks of different complexity. Profit-maximizing AI providers set the price of AI, and AI systems improve through task-specific learning from deployment. In an initial technological state where labor has the comparative advantage at complex tasks, the providers' profit maximization incentives suppress AI deployment on complex tasks, even though these are most valuable for frontier learning. I characterize when this tension gives rise to an accelerating path of AI adoption or a learning trap. Competition can accelerate AI adoption relative to monopoly by shifting AI deployment toward more complex tasks, which boosts frontier learning. Asymmetric competition can further accelerate AI adoption by inducing providers to specialize, which concentrates complex-task data.
item.dc:creator: Carl-Christian Groh

item.title: Monotone Allocations without Single-Crossing: When to Bunch and When to Jump
item.description: arXiv:2608.19474v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study one-dimensional screening when the Spence-Mirrlees condition fails along a monotone dividing curve, on which all types value marginal output equally. A single ratio, marginal distortion over marginal rent, governs the problem. When the relaxed solution stays in the positive region, non-decreasing optima in the positive single-crossing region are continuous if the ratio increases in the decision. When it crosses a flat curve and marginal rents are separable, every continuous contract is improved by a jump. When it crosses a strictly monotone curve, a contract that pools and jumps continues along the mirror of the pool if the ratio does not increase along it. Optimality among all implementable allocations, deterministic or random, is proved by a measure on the binding constraints whose weights are the same ratio; with constant curvatures and no crossing, it is also necessary. As applications, we solve problems of procurement and nonlinear pricing.
item.dc:creator: Aloisio Araujo, Carolina Parra, Sergei Vieira

item.title: Suspicious Perfection: Rating Rewards, Credibility Inversion, and Information Loss
item.description: arXiv:2608.24062v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Platforms use rating bonuses and badges to reward good sellers. When ratings can be inflated, stronger rewards can instead weaken the information available to buyers. We study an initially informative rating system in which sellers can pay to raise their displayed score and buyers rationally account for manipulation. Manipulation costs and returns are common across qualities conditional on the honest rating. Under this restriction, credibility can fail to increase between adjacent scores only where the higher score earns an additional reward. Our main result concerns large top-rating bonuses. Once sellers choose only between keeping their honest rating and reaching the top, a larger bonus makes the equilibrium rating system less informative in Blackwell's order along either extremal equilibrium selection. Lower scores retain their honest quality composition but become rarer. As the bonus grows, almost everyone displays the top score, its credibility approaches the population average, and the value of rating information vanishes. Nevertheless, a nearly perfect score can remain more credible than a perfect one. We derive the rate of information loss for exponential manipulation costs and establish a budget-feasible exposure rule that avoids credibility reversals. The results suggest that platform evaluations should examine rating frequencies together with category credibility. Rational buyer skepticism can correct the interpretation of ratings without recovering the distinctions that manipulation has erased.
item.dc:creator: Van-Quy Nguyen

item.title: Contracting for Decision-Relevant Beliefs
item.description: arXiv:2609.23285v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An expert may misreport her forecast to influence a decision she cares about. We study contracts that elicit both her belief about a verifiable state and her stake in a binary action. If every belief is possible at two distinct stakes, exact incentive compatibility prevents a belief-only mechanism from letting the action depend on the report. Asking about both belief and stake allows the action to respond, but may require implementation rent. For threshold rules, we show that minimum rent equals the cutoff's positive curvature weighted by the belief distribution. The principal therefore chooses a cutoff by balancing virtual surplus against the implementation rent of truthful reporting. We characterize the best cutoff rule and give sufficient conditions under which it is optimal even among randomized mechanisms.
item.dc:creator: Bo Cowgill

item.title: Large player classes and approximately weighted voting
item.description: arXiv:2610.08968v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: It is known that completeness of the coalitional ($C$-)desirability relation in a simple game does not imply the existence of a weighted-majority representation. We show that weightedness is implied in an approximate sense. Call an $n$-player simple game $\varepsilon$-weighted if, for some weight vector in the $(n-1)$-simplex, any losing coalition weight exceeds any winning coalition weight by at most $\varepsilon$; let $\varepsilon^{\ast}$ be the smallest such $\varepsilon$. We establish an upper bound on $\varepsilon^{\ast}$ in a general $C$-complete game, and deduce that, if all classes of equally desirable players become large asymptotically but the number of classes is bounded, then $\varepsilon^{\ast}=O(1/n_{\min})$ for the minimal player class size $n_{\min}$, and the bound is tight. Importantly, the minimal attainable fraction $\delta$ of coalitions mislabeled by a weighting rule also tends to $0$ when $n_{\min}\rightarrow\infty$ and the number of player classes is bounded, with $\delta=O(1/\sqrt{n_{\min}})$.
item.dc:creator: Ezra Einy, Ori Haimanko

item.title: Dynamic Mechanism and Information Design in AI-Agent Environments: A General Analytical Framework
item.description: arXiv:2610.11177v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper develops a general framework for dynamic mechanism and information design with AI agents, encompassing optimal contracting and integrating evolving hidden information and hidden action with partial verification, technological authorization, and multi-agent interaction. It nests conventional dynamic screening, hidden-action contracting, and conditional dynamic information design, while allowing reporting, action, and information-use decisions to interact through a common continuation mechanism. We establish a dynamic revelation principle and a recursive characterization of implementability in which truthful reporting and post-report obedience are jointly determined through continuation incentives. In quasilinear optimal-contracting environments, dynamic envelope and integral-monotonicity methods yield a verification-adjusted dynamic virtual-surplus representation and identify three distinct margins: dynamic information rents, verification rents, and the implementation cost of hidden action. These margins generate a branched hierarchy separating conventional dynamic screening, hidden-action contracting, and their joint problem. We also study the joint design of monitoring, information use, and incentives: more informative monitoring capacity expands the designer's opportunity set, but full disclosure need not be optimal, and information use can itself alter hidden-action incentives. With multiple agents, correlated information, peer discipline, coupled incentives, joint feasibility, and continuation opportunities create additional strategic interactions. Although motivated by AI-agent environments, the framework applies more broadly to dynamic agency settings with similar economic features.
item.dc:creator: Guoqiang Tian

item.title: Overcoming unfairness via repeated interactions in mini-ultimatum game
item.description: arXiv:2604.03625v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Repeated interactions are ubiquitous and known to promote social behaviour. While research often focuses on cooperation in the Prisoner's Dilemma, experimental evidence suggests repeated interactions also foster fairness. This study addresses a gap in the literature by theoretically modelling the evolution of fairness within a repeated mini-ultimatum game. Specifically, we construct a repeated-game framework where offerers and accepters interact using reactive strategies. We then investigate whether fair reactive strategy pairs are resilient against unfair mutants in a two-species population. By analyzing short-term evolutionary stability via the concept of two-species evolutionary stable strategy, we identify a critical effective game length: below this value, fairness is promoted by offerers and accepters who comply with their partner's past actions. Above this critical value, fairness is maintained by `complier' offerers and fair accepters. We also show that specific reactive strategies effectively facilitate the emergence and sustenance of fairness in long-term mutation-selection dynamics. To this end, we develop a two-population stochastic dynamics model -- a generalization of classical adaptive dynamics -- that accounts for finite population sizes and non-local mutants in the reactive strategy space.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Physica A: Statistical Mechanics and its Applications 702 (2026) 132110
item.dc:creator: Prosanta Mandal, Arunava Patra, Sagar Chakraborty

item.title: AI Model Design and Physician Liability
item.description: arXiv:2608.13618v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Clinical algorithms can perform differently across patient groups, a concern that grows as these algorithms increasingly take the form of artificial intelligence (AI) models. In the United States, a 2024 federal rule bars healthcare providers that receive federal funds from discriminating through their use of clinical algorithms, which exposes them to liability when such use disadvantages a protected patient group. We examine how such liability considerations reshape (i) an AI firm's model design decisions that drive group-specific accuracy and (ii) a physician's decisions to use AI in healthcare delivery. The firm designs an AI model for two patient groups, and improving accuracy for the disadvantaged group is more costly. The physician (who remains the accountable decision maker) then decides whether to consult AI, weighing the reduction in clinical uncertainty against expected liability exposure when AI errors disproportionately affect the disadvantaged group. We find that this liability can induce disparate use of AI: the physician may reduce AI use overall and, over an intermediate range of liability, rely on AI less for disadvantaged patients. The effect is non-monotone. As liability increases, the physician's use of AI for disadvantaged patients first declines, then rises as the firm reallocates investment toward reducing disparity or switches to an equal-accuracy design. Mandating equal algorithmic accuracy across patient groups can then inadvertently harm both groups, because a uniform accuracy requirement distorts the firm's investment incentives and the physician's equilibrium AI-use decisions.

item.title: When One Leak Pays Forever: Context Binding and the Price of Deterring Collusion
item.description: arXiv:2609.36667v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A coalition that deviates once can profit many times when what it sells keeps working. In a threshold-encrypted mempool, a leading defense against maximal extractable value (MEV), a quorum of the decryption committee that sells its decryption capability to a front-runner exposes every later block that the capability still decrypts. We ask how large a penalty, such as slashable stake, deters this kind of collusion. In our repeated game, a single leak by any coalition in a monotone family of authorized coalitions (for example, any $k$ of the $n$ committee members) unlocks a set of future rounds, costs a one-time penalty, and ends the coalition's participation. We show that every dynamic deviation reduces to choosing a leak time, so deterrence holds if and only if each coalition's penalty covers the largest discounted value that a single leak reaches. Without discounting, over $T$ rounds of unit value full reuse needs a penalty of $T$ while binding each leak to its own round needs $1$, so no penalty that is constant in the horizon deters unbounded reuse; a reuse window of $w$ rounds costs at most $w$ times the largest per-round value. The cheapest profile of per-party stakes that deters every coalition solves a covering linear program. For blockchain design, per-epoch keys cut the required stake from the value of a key's lifetime to the value of one epoch; we calibrate the gap on Ethereum front-running data and place Ferveo and Shutter in the model. The analysis extends to sealed-bid auctions, multi-authority voting, and federated learning under a shared key.
